about: Oldest laws, documents and maps of the isles: law codes and laws still in force, charters, records of government and the oldest maps, each with quoted sources; researched 2026-10-27.

entries.name: Law of Æthelberht
entries.age_text: c. 600 (early 7th century); only copy in the Textus Roffensis of the early 1120s
entries.claim: The first law code in a Germanic language, and the earliest datable text composed in English
entries.evidence: About ninety laws of King Æthelberht of Kent, mostly a tariff of compensations, thought to have been written down soon after the conversion of Kent. No original survives: the only copy is in the Textus Roffensis, compiled at Rochester half a millennium later, so its wording may have been updated in copying. It is the oldest of the English law codes that follow it (Hlothhere and Eadric, Wihtred, Ine, Alfred).

sources.title: Law of Æthelberht
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It originates in the kingdom of Kent, and is the first Germanic-language law code.

entries.name: Senchas Már (Brehon law)
entries.age_text: tracts written down from the 7th century; collected in the 8th century
entries.claim: The largest collection of early Irish (Brehon) law, among the oldest law texts of Ireland
entries.evidence: Early Irish law was the work of professional jurists (brehons); its oldest surviving tracts were first written down in the seventh century and gathered into the Senchas Már in the eighth, though its prologue claims the time of St Patrick. The texts survive in much later manuscripts, mostly of the 14th to 16th centuries, and dates for individual tracts vary. Brehon law stayed in use in much of Ireland until it was replaced by English common law in the 17th century.

sources.title: Senchas Már
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: is the largest collection of early Irish legal texts, compiled into a single group sometime in the 8th century, though individual tracts vary in date

sources.title: Early Irish law

entries.name: Laws of Hywel Dda (Cyfraith Hywel)
entries.age_text: traditionally codified mid-10th century; earliest manuscripts 13th century
entries.claim: The native law of medieval Wales; its oldest manuscript, Peniarth 28, is the earliest surviving copy
entries.evidence: Welsh law is said to have been codified under Hywel Dda in the mid-10th century, but that rests on tradition: no manuscript survives from before the 13th century, and the surviving texts show regional differences and later revision. Peniarth 28, a Latin text with drawings of the king and his officers, is generally taken as the earliest copy; the National Library of Wales dates it to the middle of the 13th century, Wikipedia to the second half.

sources.quote: according to tradition, only first codified during the reign of Hywel Dda in the mid-10th century. The earliest surviving manuscripts, however, are in Latin, date from the early 13th century

entries.name: Statute of Marlborough
entries.claim: The oldest statute law still in force in the United Kingdom
entries.evidence: Passed at Marlborough under Henry III; four of its 29 chapters, about distress (seizing goods for debt) and waste, remain in force, one of them retitled the Distress Act 1267 in 1948. The Law Commission has proposed repealing two of them. Older rules survive as common law rather than statute; the oldest statutes in force elsewhere in the isles are the Fairs Act 1204 in Ireland and the Royal Mines Act 1424 in Scotland.

sources.quote: Those four chapters constitute the oldest piece of statute law in the United Kingdom still in force

entries.name: Charter of Hlothhere to Reculver
entries.claim: The oldest Anglo-Saxon charter surviving as an original
entries.evidence: King Hlothhere of Kent granted land on Thanet and at Sturry to Abbot Beorhtwald and his minster at Reculver; the charter was written at Reculver and kept in the archive of Christ Church, Canterbury. The original is British Library Cotton Augustus ii. 2 (Wikipedia places it in the Canterbury Cathedral archive, the Sawyer catalogue in the British Library). Older charters survive only as later copies, and many of those are interpolated or forged.

entries.name: William Charter to the City of London
entries.claim: The oldest document in the City of London's archive, and apparently the earliest royal document guaranteeing the collective rights of a town's inhabitants
entries.evidence: A strip of vellum about six inches by one and a half, written in Old English, in which William the Conqueror confirms to the bishop, the portreeve and the burgesses of London the rights they had under Edward the Confessor. It has been kept by the City ever since. The claim to be the first guarantee of a town's collective rights is UNESCO's, phrased as 'appears to be'.

sources.title: William Charter to the City of London
sources.author: The London Archives
sources.quote: is the oldest document in the City's archive, given by King William I (the Conqueror) to the City in 1067

sources.author: UK National Commission for UNESCO
sources.locator: Memory of the World UK Register, 2010
sources.quote: The Charter appears to be the earliest royal or imperial document which guarantees the collective rights of the inhabitants of any town.

entries.name: Charter of Duncan II
entries.evidence: Duncan II, king for about six months in 1094, granted Tyninghame and other lands in Lothian to the monks of St Cuthbert at Durham, whose archive still holds the original. It is his only surviving charter; there is no sign the grant took effect, and his half-brother Edgar later made a similar one.

sources.quote: It was he who granted the earliest surviving Scottish charter.

entries.name: Domesday Book
entries.age_text: survey 1085–86 (completion of the book possibly later)
entries.claim: The oldest public record in England, and The National Archives' earliest surviving public record
entries.evidence: The record of William the Conqueror's survey of who held land in England and parts of Wales before and after 1066. Its colophon dates the survey to 1086, but when the book itself was written is debated, and one recent study argues it may not have been completed until 1098–1114. Older records of government survive elsewhere in fragments and copies; Domesday is the oldest held in the public records.

entries.name: Pipe Rolls
entries.age_text: earliest roll 1129–30; nearly continuous from 1155–56 to 1832
entries.claim: The oldest continuous series of records of English government
entries.evidence: The annual audit of the sheriffs' and others' accounts at the Exchequer. The roll of 1129–30 is the earliest to survive, already in a mature form, and an extract from one of 1124 is known; the series then runs almost unbroken from 1155 until 1832, with only four rolls missing. Ireland's earliest surviving pipe roll is of 1212.

sources.title: Pipe rolls
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: They form the oldest continuous series of records concerning English governance

sources.title: Medieval financial records: pipe rolls 1130-c.1300

entries.name: Aberdeen Burgh Registers
entries.claim: The earliest and most complete surviving records of any Scottish town
entries.evidence: The council registers ('common books') of Aberdeen survive from 1398, recording elections, burgess admissions, property and disputes; the third volume (about 1414–34) has been lost. The first eight volumes are on the UK Memory of the World Register. Scotland's national records of government suffered heavy losses, which makes this run exceptional.

entries.name: Tynwald
entries.claim: Claims to be the oldest continuous parliament in the world
entries.evidence: The parliament of the Isle of Man, of Norse origin, still meets in the open air at Tynwald Hill, St John's, every July. The date 979 was chosen for the millennium of 1979 without evidence; the place-name is first recorded in the 13th–14th century Chronicles of Mann. Iceland's Althing is older but was interrupted, which is why Tynwald's claim is to unbroken existence.

sources.title: Tynwald
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Established in 979 according to tradition or in the 13th century according to available historical evidence, it is the oldest continuous legislature in the world

entries.name: Ptolemy's map of the British Isles
entries.age_text: c. AD 150 (coordinates); oldest surviving drawn copies c. 1300
entries.claim: The oldest known map of the British Isles, preserved as coordinates and redrawn in later manuscripts
entries.evidence: Ptolemy's Geography, written at Alexandria in the 2nd century, listed places of the known world by latitude and longitude, including Britain (Albion) and Ireland (Hibernia). No ancient drawing survives: the oldest maps were redrawn from the numbers by Maximos Planudes' team in Constantinople a little before 1300, with Scotland turned sharply to the east. Whether Ptolemy himself drew maps is debated.

sources.title: Medieval Maps of Britain
sources.author: Medievalists.net
sources.quote: producing the earliest surviving Greek manuscript tradition with a full set of Ptolemaic maps. This includes a map of the British Isles.

sources.title: Ptolemy's Geography
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The three earliest surviving texts with maps are those from Constantinople (Istanbul) based on Planudes's work.

entries.name: Anglo-Saxon Cotton world map
entries.claim: One of the earliest surviving maps to show the British Isles in a recognisable way
entries.evidence: A world map in a manuscript of Priscian's geography (Cotton Tiberius B. V, fol. 56v), probably made at or near Canterbury, once dated to the 990s. Britain and Ireland appear as distinct islands with London, Winchester and Dublin marked. Earlier world maps label Britannia and Hibernia (the map linked to Abbo of Fleury, c. 1000) or may show Britain as a blot (the 8th-century Albi map), so it is not the first depiction, only one of the first recognisable ones.

sources.title: Medieval Maps of Britain
sources.author: Medievalists.net
sources.quote: one of the earliest surviving maps to depict the British Isles in a recognisable way

sources.title: Early world maps
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: more recent analysis indicates that, although the information was revised about that time, the map was probably drawn between 1025 and 1050

entries.name: Matthew Paris's maps of Britain
entries.claim: The earliest surviving maps of Great Britain on its own
entries.evidence: Matthew Paris, a monk of St Albans, drew four maps of Britain in his chronicles in the 1250s, with north at the top and over 250 place-names, laid out as a guide rather than to scale. They predate the Gough Map by about a century; the sources call his the first English map of Britain, but none states in so many words that no earlier map of Britain survives.

sources.title: Medieval Maps of Britain
sources.author: Medievalists.net
sources.quote: produced a map of Britain in the 1250s. It survives in four manuscripts

sources.title: Christopher Saxton's Atlas (Book of the Month, June 2002)

entries.name: Gough Map
entries.age_text: conventionally c. 1360; recent studies 1370s to early 15th century
entries.claim: The earliest surviving map to show routes across Britain and a recognisable coastline; the earliest known sheet map of Britain
entries.evidence: A map of Britain on two sheepskins in the Bodleian Library, with red lines and distances between towns. Its long-accepted date of about 1360 is now in doubt: studies of handwriting and spectral imaging suggest it was made in the 1370s and revised into the 15th century, or drawn in layers from about 1390 onwards. Matthew Paris's maps of Britain are older, but the Gough Map is the first with a recognisable outline.

sources.title: The Gough Map
sources.author: UK National Commission for UNESCO
sources.locator: Memory of the World UK Register, 2011
sources.quote: Dated approximately 1360, it is the earliest surviving map to show routes across Britain and to depict a recognisable coastline.

sources.title: About the Gough Map

sources.quote: The Gough Map is the earliest known sheet map of Britain, noted for its remarkable accuracy, particularly in south east England

sources.title: Gough Map
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: One study concludes that the map must have been made in the early years of the fifteenth century, while another suggests that the map was produced in the 1370s but extensively revised, perhaps as late as 1430.

entries.name: Saxton's Atlas of England and Wales
entries.age_text: surveyed 1574–78; published as an atlas in 1579
entries.claim: The first county maps of England and Wales, often called the first national atlas of any country
entries.evidence: Christopher Saxton surveyed every county of England and Wales with the backing of Thomas Seckford and Lord Burghley; the sheets were printed separately from 1574 and issued together with a general map in 1579. Mercator's map of the British Isles (1564) is older but is a single map; Saxton's maps were the basis of English county maps for over a century.
